header:
Date: 2026-09-05
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 34 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Patel (Emberfield - Head ML Ops), Danielle Ruiz (CTO), Marco Lorenzi (Infra Lead)
summary: Intro meeting to map Emberfield's expected token volumes, latency targets, and compliance constraints. Focus on hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, per-token economics, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and initial pilot scoping.
topics: Current stack; Expected QPS and token-per-request; Budget ceilings; Latency SLOs; Data residency/KMS/SSO; Pilot scope and next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're Maya from Redwood, and Liam our SE is here. quick intros?
[00:12] Danielle: Danielle, CTO, hi. we're looking at pushing more model features into our claims intake flow.
[00:18] Sofia: Sofia, head of ML Ops. main concern is cost predictability and data residency.
[00:22] Marco: Marco, infra. we'll own networking and KMS.
[00:27] Liam: great, thanks. goal for today is to understand your volume and what success looks like, then walk through how hosted/dedicated/private change the unit economics.
[00:36] Danielle: sounds good. high level numbers first: our pilot is ~250k requests/day, average prompt + response ~1.4k tokens, spikes to 400 RPS during business hours.
[00:49] Sofia: besides that, we have a hard monthly budget of $25k for this initiative in year one.
[00:55] Maya: okay that helps. so 250k * 1.4k tokens = roughly 350M tokens/day, wait that seems high, let me recalc — sorry, brain lag. if each request is 1.4k tokens, 250k requests/day -> 350M tokens/day, yep. monthly would be ~10.5B tokens.
[01:15] Danielle: yikes, that was our estimate but we might compress prompts and use shorter responses for prod. pilot is more like 50k/day.
[01:23] Sofia: yes pilot target 50k/day to start, but we want headroom planning for 250k.
[01:28] Liam: good — so two scenarios: pilot (50k/day) and scale (250k/day). host vs dedicated delta typically changes per-token price and adds fixed reserved cost. let me give a conceptual breakdown.
[01:44] Liam: Hosted: no infra to manage, pay per token; good for fast time-to-value. Dedicated: reserved GPU capacity — lower per-token compute cost but you pay a fixed monthly fee for the pool. Private: similar to dedicated but customer-managed control plane, so higher setup cost but meets residency/KMS requirements.
[02:01] Marco: for private, we need the option to bring-your-own-HSM and run everything in our VPC. Is that supported?
[02:07] Liam: yes, private supports KMS/HSM integrations and VPC modes. we documented the network ports and peering steps; i'll share the checklist.
[02:14] Maya: on pricing levers, key things are: model choice, quantization, batching, and caching. caching here means prefix (static prompt) caching and KV cache reuse for sessions. those can reduce per-token compute by up to 30-60% depending on your workload.
[02:28] Sofia: can you give a concrete example?
[02:31] Liam: sure. imagine two patterns: 1) long form claims summary — each request 2k tokens and little reuse; 2) templated Q&A — prompts share 60% same prefix. with prefix caching and KV reuse, effective compute tokens drop because redwood can reuse cached KV for the prefix and only compute for added tokens, which for Q&A reduces compute by ~50% on our observed workloads.
[02:55] Danielle: how does batching play in? we have latency SLOs of <300ms p50 for user-facing UI.
[03:02] Liam: batching increases throughput and lowers per-token cost but adds latency. Redwood's continuous batching tries to keep batching windows small and adaptive. for strict 300ms p50, we still see benefits from small batch sizes — maybe 2–4 requests combined — which gives modest savings (10–20%) while meeting SLOs. for background jobs you can use larger batch windows and better unit econ.
[03:22] Marco: what's dedicated reserved sizing look like? we want to avoid paying too much during pilot.
[03:27] Maya: dedicated is flexible; you can reserve a modest pool for pilot and enable autoscale burst to hosted for spikes. commit tiers come at month commitments. typical pilot pool might be a single A30-equivalent host (or multi-GPU slice) depending on model and peak concurrency — we'll run a sizing calc after we get sample traces.
[03:43] Sofia: about cost numbers — can you ballpark per-token for hosted today?
[03:47] Liam: cautious ballpark — hosted for a mid-sized open LLM we often price in the few dollars per million token range, say $3–6 per 1M tokens depending on model size and perf. dedicated effective compute cost can be 20–40% lower once you amortize the reserved pool across volume, but you add fixed monthly. private adds some integration/ops fees. these are example ranges; we'll produce a worked pilot worksheet.
[04:09] Danielle: so for our pilot 50k/day ~ 1.4k tokens * 50k = 70M tokens/day or 2.1B/month. at $4 per 1M tokens that's $8.4k/month in hosted compute alone — within the $25k budget but leaves room for overhead.
[04:28] Maya: exact — and with caching and batching we can likely halve compute for templated flows, so pilot might be closer to $4k–6k in hosted costs depending on pattern.
[04:36] Sofia: what about latency variation across hosting modes?
[04:39] Liam: hosted is multi-tenant but optimized; p50/p95 depends on model and region. dedicated gives more stable tail latencies. private depends heavily on your network and infra choices — e.g., if you provision in-region GPUs and avoid cross-AZ egress, you can match dedicated latency. we have guidance for colocating model hosts and the control plane.
[04:59] Marco: are logs and audit trails available for hosted? we need detailed per-request audit for compliance.
[05:03] Liam: yes, hosted exposes audit logs (request metadata, model version, latency, token counts) and you can export to your SIEM. for Private, you control log retention and storage.
[05:11] Danielle: and encryption at rest? key rotation?
[05:14] Liam: SOC2 standard, data encrypted at rest. private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM with rotation policies. we'll send the security deck.
[05:22] Sofia: about fallback policies — do you support automatic fallbacks to smaller/cheaper models to stay within budget?
[05:27] Maya: yes, routing policy can route by cost or latency tiers. you can set up an A/B or fallback where something goes to a cheaper distilled model if cost threshold hit. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization or alternative models per workload.
[05:39] Marco: how much engineering work to integrate with our SSO and SAML?
[05:43] Liam: minimal for hosted — SAML SSO plus SCIM for provisioning. private includes SSO but requires network setup. we have a solutions guide and our SE will help run the integration.
[05:53] Danielle: what's the pilot timeline? we want production in Q4 if feasible.
[05:57] Maya: typical pilot 4–8 weeks: week 1-2 sizing and security review, week 3 small pilot, week 4 review and expand. if private, add a provisioning window of 2–4 weeks for networking and KMS.
[06:10] Sofia: ok, could you show a quick worked example of unit econ combining batching/caching?
[06:14] Liam: sure. quick calcs — assume pilot 50k/day, 1.4k tokens/request = 70M tokens/day -> 2.1B tokens/month. base hosted price $4 per 1M -> $8.4k/month. now apply caching for templated flows — 40% of requests reuse a 60% prefix; effective compute reduction 24% overall. bring cost to ~$6.4k. with small batching savings of 12% more, you land near ~$5.6k. that's illustrative.
[06:43] Danielle: nice. are there tooling hooks where we can see which prompts are cacheable?
[06:47] Liam: yes, Redwood Console surfaces token-level breakdowns, per-route cache hit rates, and a prompt clustering view to help identify templated prefixes. we'll share screenshots.
[06:56] Sofia: regulatory question: we need data residency in EU for EU customers. can hosted do EU-only storage and compute?
[07:02] Liam: hosted supports region pins; compute and logs can be restricted to EU regions. for strict residency the private deployment is usually chosen.
[07:09] Marco: network specifics: port 443 egress, mTLS? we want peering not public egress.
[07:13] Liam: we support VPC peering and private link options; we'll send the network matrix.
[07:20] Maya: circling back to budget constraints: given your $25k/mo overall, pilot hosted ~$6k, some engineering + audit overhead one time — should fit. if you scale to 250k/day, numbers grow; that's where dedicated becomes attractive. we'll run a dedicated vs hosted ROI with your traces.
[07:35] Danielle: concerning dedicated, what are typical minimum commits?
[07:38] Maya: depends but you can start with a small pool; often the minimum practical commit for large models is a monthly pool in the low tens of k USD. we'll put concrete options in the worksheet.
[07:47] Sofia: what's the SLA on dedicated for latency/uptime?
[07:50] Liam: dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we can share the SLA pdf.
[07:55] Marco: on billing, do you support cost allocation tags per team?
[07:58] Maya: yes tagging and per-token allocation by API key and route with console breakdowns.
[08:05] Danielle: ok next steps recap?
[08:07] Maya: we'll send the pilot worksheet with worked unit-econ scenarios, security docs, and a private deployment checklist. we'll request 48h of traces and propose the technical deep-dive slot.
[08:18] Sofia: great. thank you.
[08:20] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with materials and a proposed calendar for the deep dive.
[08:26] Danielle: bye.

NOTE: Transcription contains occasional mis-attributions and filler words. Numbers and ranges are illustrative; the team will provide formal pricing and a worked spreadsheet.
